query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase titanium–nickel high‐entropy alloy, the addition of a low concentration of molybdenum (Mo) will improve elevated‐temperature mechanical performance relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, solid‐solution high‐entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a low concentration of Mo during alloy fabrication.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures under extreme or oxidizing environments, using identical processing and heat‐treatment for both variants.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced stabilization of the solid‐solution state and a refined microstructure due to Mo’s incorporation.
generation.mechanism: Mo, as a high-melting-point refractory element, increases the effective melting point and reinforces solid solution strengthening by reducing impurity-induced segregation and hindering dislocation motion, which retards creep and improves yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-alloyed variant is expected to exhibit higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The original titanium–nickel high‐entropy alloy produced without any Mo addition.
generation.boundary: Mo addition is limited to a low concentration to ensure retention of the single-phase solid-solution; testing is confined to elevated-temperature regimes that simulate extreme or oxidizing service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While improvement is expected, the precise magnitude of the mechanical performance enhancement remains uncertain and is likely to depend on the exact Mo concentration and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens using identical fabrication and heat-treatment protocols: one set of the baseline Ti–Ni alloy and one set with a low concentration of Mo added. Subject both sets to identical elevated-temperature mechanical tests, such as tensile or creep testing in extreme or oxidizing atmospheres.
measurements: Phase stability and microstructural characterization (via XRD, SEM, and TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-modified alloy fails to display a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures, or if secondary phases indicating loss of single-phase stability are present, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Microstructural stability is one of the most important factors for alloys to be used at elevated temperatures. A stable alloy can maintain its properties without substantial changes, even after extended periods of service (). The minor presence of impurity interstitials, e.g., nitrogen and oxygen, in the equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy studied was found to introduce uncertainties in its mechanical properties at the aging temperature by facilitating phase segregation at the nanoscale and reducing the solid strengthening effect. Furthermore, the depletion of impurity interstitials in regions adjacent to grain boundaries leads to the formation of PFZs. This spatially confined compositional variation nearby grain boundaries creates very high local electrochemical and mechanical contrast, often affecting the alloy’s corrosion and mechanical properties (). To improve the stability of RHEAs for high-temperature applications, the impurities must be better controlled. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures. This strengthening mechanism is explained with the change of deformation mode from screw to edge dislocations, which contributes an edge-dislocation-induced strength. drafts.hypothesis: A precisely timed aging heat treatment that induces the in‐situ formation of fine, coherent Ni3Ti precipitates in the single‐phase Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature strength and creep resistance compared to the untreated, as-cast alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: Titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state
drafts.intervention: Apply a post-synthesis aging heat treatment at a temperature below the onset of primary phase decomposition (e.g., approximately 700–800°C) for a controlled duration designed to promote the nucleation and growth of nano-scale Ni3Ti intermetallic precipitates.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing conditions, such as tensile and creep tests performed between 750°C and 900°C.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale, coherent Ni3Ti precipitates dispersed uniformly within the matrix
drafts.mechanism: The precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby enhancing strength and improving creep resistance at elevated temperatures through a precipitate-hardening mechanism.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The heat-treated alloy will exhibit significantly improved tensile strength and creep resistance under high-temperature conditions relative to the as-cast, single-phase alloy.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast, fully solid-solution Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy without any post-synthesis heat treatment.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to compositions in which titanium and nickel are present as primary constituents in a single-phase solid-solution state; the effect may differ for alloys already exhibiting secondary phases or significant compositional variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to the proposed aging heat treatment while keeping the other set as the as-cast control. Perform identical high-temperature tensile and creep tests on both sets. Conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM) to confirm the formation of fine Ni3Ti precipitates in the treated samples.
measurements: Tensile strength at temperatures between 750°C and 900°C
Creep rate and time to failure under sustained high-temperature loading
Microstructural characterization (e.g., precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in tensile strength and creep resistance compared to the as-cast samples, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the expected Ni3Ti precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Applying an optimized aging heat‐treatment to induce fine, coherent Ti–Ni precipitates in the high‐entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical performance compared to its as-cast, solid-solution state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A titanium–nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid solution (as-cast state) with titanium and nickel as primary constituents.
drafts.intervention: A controlled aging heat-treatment following solution treatment, designed to nucleate and grow fine, coherent precipitates within the matrix.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature testing conditions (e.g., in the range of 700–900 °C) and/or extreme-environment exposure (such as oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres) relevant to the alloy’s intended applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: Fine, coherent Ti–Ni precipitates dispersed throughout the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The induced precipitates will act as barriers to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding under high-temperature conditions, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance relative to the untreated solid-solution alloy.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy is expected to exhibit statistically significant improvements in yield strength and/or creep resistance under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing compared to the baseline as-cast material.
drafts.baseline: The original, as-cast single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy without any post-solidification heat-treatment intervention.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to high-entropy alloys where titanium and nickel are primary constituents in a single-phase solid solution; the elevated-temperature performance is evaluated under test regimes around 700–900 °C and in relevant extreme-environment conditions. The effect size, while expected to be significant, is uncertain in magnitude and may depend on precise aging parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens of the target high-entropy alloy: one group receives the solution treatment followed by the optimized aging heat-treatment to induce precipitate formation, and the second group is left in the as-cast state. Both groups are then subjected to identical elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., yield strength measurement, creep testing) under controlled atmospheres.
measurements: Creep rate under constant load at elevated temperatures
Microstructural characterization (via TEM or SEM) to confirm precipitate formation in the aged samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., higher yield strength and lower creep rate) compared to the as-cast baseline, or if the precipitate morphology does not correlate with improved mechanical properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of molybdenum (around 3-5 at.%) to a single-phase titanium–nickel-based high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical performance compared to the unmodified alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents.
drafts.intervention: Alloy modification by incorporating a minor fraction (3–5 at.%) of molybdenum into the base composition.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., 1200–1600 °C) under extreme or oxidizing environments, with identical processing and heat-treatment conditions for both variants.
drafts.structural_mediator: Stabilization of the solid-solution state via enhanced atomic bonding and reduced impurity-induced segregation at grain boundaries, leading to refined microstructure and maintained phase purity.
drafts.mechanism: Mo, as a high-melting-point refractory element, promotes stronger solid solution strengthening. It raises the effective melting point, delays impurity-induced phase segregation, and stabilizes dislocation structures by increasing the resistance to creep at high temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Mo-added alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the base titanium–nickel alloy while retaining its single-phase structure.
drafts.baseline: The original titanium–nickel-based high-entropy alloy without any Mo addition.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is limited to a low level of Mo addition (not exceeding ~5 at.%) to maintain the single-phase solid-solution and avoid the formation of secondary phases; testing is confined to elevated temperature regimes (approximately 1200–1600 °C) in oxidizing or extreme environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the base titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy and another with a 3–5 at.% Mo addition. Process both sets using identical melting and homogenization protocols to achieve a single-phase structure. Subject the samples to mechanical testing (e.g., compression or tensile tests) at temperatures between 1200 °C and 1600 °C in a controlled oxidizing atmosphere.
measurements: Creep resistance (strain rate under constant load)
Phase analysis via XRD and microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the base alloy, or if secondary phases are observed (indicating loss of single-phase stability), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐based high-entropy alloy that is initially a single-phase solid solution, the targeted introduction of a small amount of a refractory element (e.g., molybdenum) will enhance the alloy’s elevated-temperature mechanical performance compared to the unmodified alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, prepared without additional refractory elements.
drafts.intervention: Add a low concentration (e.g., ≈5 atomic percent) of molybdenum during alloy fabrication to form an augmented alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: Tests conducted under elevated-temperature regimes (e.g., 800°C to 1400°C) and/or extreme-environment conditions (oxidative or corrosive atmospheres) representative of service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to dissolve into the single-phase matrix, increasing the average melting point and promoting a refined solid solution that retards dislocation motion and alters slip behavior.
drafts.mechanism: The increased presence of a high-melting-point refractory element (Mo) is anticipated to enhance solid solution strengthening and to shift the dominant dislocation mechanism from thermally activated screw to edge dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby improving yield strength and creep resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Mo-alloyed high-entropy alloy should exhibit a higher elevated-temperature yield strength, slower creep rates, and better microstructural stability compared to the base Ti–Ni alloy without the Mo intervention.
drafts.baseline: The original titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy produced without any refractory element additions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase Ti–Ni HEAs evaluated at elevated temperatures (roughly 800°C–1400°C) and in environments where oxidizing or corrosive conditions might be encountered.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set consists of the baseline Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy and the other set includes the same alloy with ≈5 at.% Mo added. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature tensile and creep tests (e.g., at temperatures ranging from 800°C to 1400°C) along with microstructural examinations via XRD, SEM, and TEM.
measurements: Creep rate and time-to-failure under constant load
Phase stability and grain structure analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-modified alloy does not display a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength, creep resistance, or microstructural stability compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
